utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Good day, everyone. Case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to greet everyone present today, the witness, members of the Prosecution, members of the Defence, as well as all the accused. There is a decision I need to render on the admissibility of documents that concern the testimony given last Thursday. There were four documents that I will now refer to slowly. There was document P 08436, which is a death certificate. This document has been marked for identification. The Chamber is asking the Prosecution to provide it with the judicial decisions referred to in the document and mentioned at the bottom of the document, and we will make a decision, having examined the case. We admit P 08608 into evidence. We also admit into evidence the following document as requested by the Defence: P 08715. As far as this exhibit is concerned, we realise that sometimes the documents provided by the Prosecution are also documents that the Defence wants admitted into evidence. Sometimes the same exhibit could have two numbers, a P number and a D number. I'm asking the registrar on the legal officer as well as the Defence to examine this problem at a later date, but we should either give such documents one number or take into consideration the fact that the same exhibit, same document, can have a number of numbers. But for the moment, P 08715 is admitted into evidence, and we will see whether we'll have a Defence number for that. We also admit into evidence 2D 0113, but I would like the Defence to scan it by using the e-court system, because so far this has not been done. Very well. Mr. Registrar, perform your duties, the duties necessary for these four documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. [In English] The following documents are tendered with the August 24th date and admitted with today's date: P 08715; 2D 00113; P 08436 marked for identification as per your oral decision dated today, under seal; P 08608. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I also take this opportunity to inform everyone present that you will be leaving us. I believe that today is your last day. You'll be assuming another post in another international organisation. On behalf of the Judges, would I like to express my regret, or our regret, but your destiny's elsewhere. Since the beginning of this case and even during the pre-trial phase, you have performed your duties in an absolutely perfect manner, and it's with regret that I note that you will be leaving us. I wanted you to be aware of the fact. We'll be continuing with the hearing of the witness today. The cross-examination will now commence. We have six hours and 45 minutes for the cross-examination. I won't waste any more time, and without further ado, I give the floor to the Defence now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have a few questions for the witness on behalf of our client.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Witness. I'd like to ask you something in connection with the questions put to you yesterday. There was some questions put to you by the Presiding Judge, Judge Antonetti, and it concerns page 35 of the transcript, of yesterday's transcript. It concerned the Spanish Battalion's liaison officer within the HVO, and yesterday you said that you did not have a liaison officer in the headquarters of the Croatian Defence Council; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Affirmative. I did say that during sometime there was one, but the question has to do with a particular period of time in the course of which there was no liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... know whether the HVO had a liaison officer of its own, a liaison officer who cooperated with UNPROFOR and the Spanish Battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. There was some officers who were the usual ones in that particular detachment, but they were not actually liaising as such with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, with your permission, I would like to show some documents to the witness. We have hard copies for the Chamber and for the accused --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: For the witness, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This will facilitate the cross-examination. So with your permission, could we show the witness these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Could you have a look at P 05220. It's a Prosecution exhibit. I've marked it with a yellow piece of paper. I've marked the part that might be of interest to you. That's the very first document. Please have a look at that document then. Have you had a look at it? You can see a chart that was made by the Spanish Battalion. If you have a look at the yellow sticker at the beginning of the document, you'll see where the chart is. It's a blue sticker. I apologise. Have you found that sketch, that chart?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that on the upper right-hand side of the document?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: It says "The operative zone of Southeastern Herzegovina" on the map. It's a chart. Page 57 in the document. Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean by that the flowchart of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Have a look at the part where it says "HVO Mostar." It says "Liaison officer with UNPROFOR, Bozo Raguz." Have you found that? This is a sketch or a chart that was made by the Spanish Battalion.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you then have a look at the following document, which is P 02108. It's a Prosecution document. It's the next one in the bundle.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we please use the e-court system and have this document on our screens. The date is the 7th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document? It's a daily summary of information. It's a document that comes from the Spanish Battalion. Could you just find the date, the 7th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: There's a part that concerns the evacuation of a wounded Muslim as requested by a certain party. This was confirmed by the liaison officer of the HVO who liaised with the Spanish Battalion, and he was Bozo Raguz, Colonel Bozo Raguz. It was on the 7th of June, 1993. Have you found that part?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that, but there was a liaison officer that was appointed, but that doesn't mean he was always with us constantly on a standing basis. Only once in awhile. And this time it was exactly the same liaison officer that we saw in the flowchart but at the time it could have been somebody else, but it just happens that this time it is the same individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you haven't understood me. I wasn't saying that he was permanently present in your battalion, but the fact is that there was a liaison officer that the Spanish Battalion had to liaise with the HVO. I've only selected two documents in which his name is referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, it appears that a colonel, a high-ranking officer, was the official liaison officer for the HVO. He was SpaBat's official liaison officer. Did this colonel have a telephone, a walkie-talkie? Was it possible to contact him around the clock, seven days a week?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We could get in touch with headquarters and then we would ask to speak with someone, either Raguz or anybody that we would want to speak with, but we didn't have a specific interlocutor that was appointed to deal with us officially and constantly. He may have been a liaison officer, but there may have been others as well. But can you consider them to be liaison officers when they're not actually physically present at your disposal? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Spanish on English channel] ... [Interpretation] ... been mentioned in an official capacity by the HVO. Wouldn't the reaction be to immediately phone the colonel or the general rather than an ordinary private?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During my six months in Bosnia, I only came across colonels and soldiers, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So are you trying to say that all the soldiers were colonels?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. I simply meant that all the officers that we got in touch with ranked as colonels. I don't know whether they actually were colonels, but they had that rank. I never met any lieutenants or captains. Now, that does not mean they did not exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Mr. Ibrisimovic, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Could we have 6D 00033 on the screen for the witness. This is the last document in the bundle that we have provided you with. It's the very last document. That's the document. That's the very last document. It's an order.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do have both documents. I have it in English and in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I'll read it out. The interpreters can follow me. It's an order on assignment dated the 22nd of March, 1993, and in this order Mr. Bozo Raguz is appointed as a -- to the post as officer liaison with UNPROFOR as of the 22nd of March, 1993. And this is the same person referred to in the Spanish Battalion documents.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There can be no doubt. I met that colonel, and I know precisely who Colonel Raguz is, and he was -- he was appointed as such, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please have a look at the penultimate document in the bundle. It's P 02291. It's a Prosecution document. It comes from the HVO, but you also have the Spanish translation, which I think has been marked with a green sticker. Have you found that? It's a document -- have you found it? Please read out the third paragraph and forgive my Spanish, but it starts with the words in Spanish, "prente havel para contactos" [phoen].

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't hear the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph which starts with the words "prente havel para contactos." Could you read it out in Spanish. It says "Prente, HVO para contactos" [phoen].

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Faced with HVO with contacts for FVO [phoen], Mr. Berislav Pusic has been put in charge." Humo and Pusic were detached to take care of the priest. That was a literal translation from Spanish.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: It doesn't say in the transcript that Mr. Busic was there on behalf of the HVO, for contact for liaison, for liaising with UNPROFOR. Mr. Berislav Pusic had been appointed to that post. That's how it was interpreted by the interpreters in the booth, and there is a reason for which I have said this. I said on behalf of the HVO and for contact with UNPROFOR, for liaison with UNPROFOR. On behalf of HVO, Mr. Pusic is appointed. I didn't say that he had been assigned as the liaison officer for UNPROFOR. That's what it says in the document in Croatian. If you have a look at this it document, it concerns a humanitarian mission authorised by Mr. Bruno Stojic. It's a matter of permission, giving permission. It's not an order; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're speaking about the authorisations to be able to take the priest out of Mostar, is that it? And to take plasma to the Mostar hospital. Is this the document we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is the document that was used as an agreement in order to be able to take the blood plasma to the hospital in Mostar the same day lieutenant Munoz was killed and after the death of Munoz we went to the area in Mostar where the priest was to be found and this was the agreement that was signed on the day before with the permission that was granted by Mr. Bruno Stojic, and I have no idea though whether you're asking a very specific question about this authorisation. Are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: No. I just wish to confirm that it is a permission, a permit, not an order, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I just want to say, Mr. President, that when the witness read this out in Spanish, the interpretation was that Mr. Pusic was appointed as a contact person. So it's not an order. The document does not represent an order. And paragraph 13 of the indictment and paragraph 13 of the pre-trial Prosecution brief, that's what it refers to, and footnote 61 of the pre-trial brief where the Prosecutor wrote that Mr. Pusic was appointed liaison officer, whereas quite obviously this was not an order, and the liaison officer was somebody quite different, quite another person. It says, "Appointed Berislav Pusic as an HVO liaison officer to UNPROFOR," in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I wonder whether there is not a problem with the translation, because in the English-speaking translation I read: "On behalf of HVO, Mr. Berislav Pusic is appointed as liaison officer with UNPROFOR." End of citation. And in that sense I read this -- this document as being -- and being labelled a permission, but it has also an element of an order, because, for instance, it will serve as an order to roadblocks which control traffic, and by showing this permission, these roadblocks are ordered to let the vehicles pass. So I think it's -- it's difficult to say it is this but not that. It is this and that, rather. But I stand to be corrected. I'm just trying to understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, in addition to that point which is similar to the one that I was going to make, there's two other points. Further on this particular document it appears that counsel again is asking this witness to interpret what Mr. Stojic meant, and as Judge Trechsel just mentioned the document speaks for itself and beyond that again, counsel is doing nothing more than asking this officer, a Spanish officer, an officer in a different army to interpret apparently what he thinks Bruno Stojic meant when he signed the document. That's objection number two. Objection number 3, Your Honour, is to the procedure. I don't it's proper, with all respect to my learned friend, to engage in argument while we have a witness on the stand. He can put his questions to the witness, he can make his point, but then to stop as we go and say, by I way I want to make my argument now and refer to particular parts in the indictment. I don't think that's proper examination and I'm concerned frankly, Your Honour, more generally that we go further -- as each day goes by we go further and further into strange and diverse practices where people are popping up at any time expressing opinions, making comments, and I would object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Now, permission in the B/C/S, I take note of the fact that this document was sent to Canarias, to the interpretation or translation service, because we have the 11th of May at 12.15, apparently, when Carlos has translated the document from the B/C/S into Spanish, and the Spanish translation is the text. Now, since the witness is here, all we have to do is to ask him to read this out in his own language and to tell us how the Spanish interpret the document. So, Witness, you have this document, the translation of it in Spanish, in your own language. So tell us how you understand it. How do you understand this document? What does it mean? What does it say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we understood this document to be was a written permission by the ministry of defence to allow movement at that time on that day to carry or ferry blood to the Mostar hospital. It was an HVO permission pursuant to the agreements negotiated the day before, and we needed, therefore, permission so that our armoured cars could show this document and be allowed through the roadblocks so as to arrive to the eastern side of Mostar. Remember that there was a conflict going on. There was a front line in Mostar which had to be crossed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you. But can you read paragraph 3 out in your own language, in Spanish. Paragraph 3, read it out in a loud voice. It begins with "Frente."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Vis-a-vis HVO for UNPROFOR contacts, Mr. Pusic is charged to deliver the priest. Mr. Umon [phoen], Mr. Pusic were in charge."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you've just read that out in Spanish, the third paragraph, and on the basis of the French translation you said that the person who was in charge for contacts with UNPROFOR was Mr. Berislav Pusic. So it does not say liaison officer it just says the person in charge of contacts in this particular case. Is that how you understood it? Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. For this specific case this person was charged. It was not the liaison officer. Once again allow me to talk about this liaison officer business, because it seems as though there was a permanent liaison officer appointed, but in practice we did not deal with one single person at headquarters, hence my saying that there was no permanent liaison officer, if this can help sort matters out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but as far as you're concerned with the plasma and things like that, if there was a problem then the person to contact in the HVO, it was Mr. Pusic, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, according to the advice received from the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, the problem that occurs is that the English translation speaks of a liaison officer. That's the term used. In the English text it says "liaison officer," whereas the person in charge of contacts, that might be somebody other than a liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I might be allowed to make an observation here. Linguistically speaking, "officer" means more than "officier" in the military sense. We can speak of an officer who is a civilian person, who performs an office, that is to say has a duty to perform. So that's what the word "Officer" can also mean in English. Perhaps the linguistic people amongst me might contradict me, but I think that that is the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The problem comes from the following fact: As we have armies, HVO and UNPROFOR, for instance, there's a liaison officer who is a military person. This -- a liaison officer is never a civilian. He's always a military person. Now, there might be a case of semantics where the liaison officer can also be a civilian, and that's what we have in this present case, it's a matter of semantics. So to distinguish this, it wasn't a colonel or general but it was Mr. Pusic. I'm going to give the floor to the Defence if they wish to belabour the point, but as far as I'm concerned we've clarified the matter now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. His Honour Judge Trechsel said this before me. What I was going to say, that it was a wrong interpretation into English, and I would like to ask the translation service to translate the document again, and then it can be tendered. That's why I made the introduction and asked the witness to read out the paragraph in Spanish. And it was the footnote -- footnote 61 was the reason that I asked the question to show that it was not an order but that it was permission. Thank you, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask the registrar to give me the calculation of time. How much time have we used for that first Defence team? And now we come to the second Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President; good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, sir. Mr. President, we have no questions for this witness. Our time, however, we would like to donate to the Praljak Defence team. We understand they have more -- need more time. So thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So your 47 minutes you're going to cede to Mr. Praljak; is that right? Counsel for Mr. Stojic, next Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. I'm going to cross-examine you now on behalf of the Defence counsel of Mr. Stojic. We still have on e-court and on our screens this document, and I'd like to have the document stay there, but before we look at the document, I'd like to ask you something else linked to this event of the 11th of May, 1993. How did you participate? In what way did you participate, you personally, in transporting this plasma from the western side to the eastern side? What was your role?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the longest-serving officer of the two armoured vehicles that were going to transport the plasma, I was in charge, although military command was exercised by Colonel Munoz who was in charge of the armoured unit. I was in charge of reaching eastern Mostar and deliver the plasma to the Muslim hospital, and later on pick up a chaplain or priest, who we didn't know where he was at the time, to bring him to the Croat or western part of Mostar. And this we did. And may I add the following that has not been heard yet: We also ferried a Muslim woman to the Croat hospital in Mostar for kidney treatment. I cannot remember her name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have a problem with the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was just waiting for the interpreters to complete the interpretation. It was a little slower. So we'll be able to understand each other better if we make pauses.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, tell me, please, Witness, whether you before this day, that is to say before the 11th of May, whether you took part in any negotiations and agreements with respect to the passage of this convoy, and did you -- do you know who in fact transported the plasma? Was it plasma going from the hospital from western Mostar? Or was it somebody else who was the organiser of the transport for the plasma? Do you know anything about that, any information along those lines?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the afternoon -- on the previous afternoon we had come with an agreement with the HVO man to allow the two armoured cars to pass through to the eastern part of Mostar. We carried the blood in the actual armoured car. There were no other vehicles involved. So we took the plasma from the Medjugorje headquarters to the Muslim hospital itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you remember whether this plasma reached Medjugorje under the International Red Cross organisation, which tried to transport plasma and some other things to eastern Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think to remember that the International Red Cross did participate because with us we had a doctor belonging to the International Red Cross. He was with us in the armoured vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When you say that you negotiated with both sides, did you take part personally in those negotiations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was not my duty nor my mission to do so. Normally its he the 5th section of the command staff that is charged with that -- with that. It wasn't my mission.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Who told you, and when, what your mission was, what you were there to do? Specifically speaking for that day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- my director chief was the one who issued the orders to me personally for the transferral of the blood, which we did, and this pursuant to military discipline.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you tell me what the order was? Did it say exactly where the plasma was to be transported, how, where the priest was, and that kind of thing? Could you summarise and paraphrase the order?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to recall exactly what the order was, but I could say transport of blood plasma to the Muslim hospital in Mostar, picking up a priest according to orders who is in a house in eastern Mostar, to ferry him to the western part of Mostar. I recall no more. I believe there was a written order which you may be able to find amongst the Spanish documents, but I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: As far as I understood it, in the mission you -- I think you said that you did something that was not included in the mission because you said that you transported a young Muslim woman from one bank to the other. I don't think that was in the mission itself, stipulated as such.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite right. When we found ourselves in the Muslim part, the Muslims asked us to take that Muslim woman who required kidney dialysis treatment, and there were no means in situ. We asked whether we could take her to the other side. We had no problem in so doing, and we believed that no problems would arise. And when it comes to the death of the lieutenant and the problem that -- that took place there, well, I took the decision to bring her with us in the armoured vehicle. I do not recall her name. And when we opened the trap door of the vehicle, the lady just left in a hurry, absolutely terrified, and we never saw her again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you say that you put the woman in the armoured vehicle, was this transport -- what -- did the HVO know about this transport or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying to remember whether we radioed our general headquarters, but I don't think so, and therefore the HVO were not informed about the presence of this woman. I don't think so. But I'm doubtful as to whether via radio from our headquarters we informed of this, but I seem to recall that there was no communication with the HVO about the fact that we were transporting this lady. And in no document will you be able to find this incident narrated because it was my personal decision at the time to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So you did have authority to take decisions of this kind. You could do that without any problems?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. Perhaps that is my phone. If it is, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So you had authorisation to be able to put somebody in your APC. You didn't have to inform anybody of that, of doing something like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, I don't remember whether via the radio I informed my superior officer of this. I don't think I did. I don't think I did. But, yes, I did have sufficient authority to take a decision involving humanitarian aid or helping a person, a civilian, that might need our help.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: May we now take a look at the permission that we have on our screens that we discussed earlier on, and I'm interested in the second sentence. Can we confirm the second sentence of this permission and -- [Spanish on English channel] ... as you state it was, or that this role concerning the transport of the priest, Ivan Vuksic. It is the second sentence in front of you, about Father Ivan Vuksic, and I'm going to read it out. It says: "Good officers of UNPROFOR will be used for transport of Father Ivan Vuksic who is at present on the left bank of the river Neretva." Is that what it says? Have I read it out properly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's so. We were meant to ferry Mr. Father Ivan Vuksic to the other side of the Neretva River.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So from this permission it would emerge that you -- it was your goodwill to do so or, rather, that you were asked by the HVO to do that while you were transporting the plasma. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I remember correctly, we had to deliver the plasma and take the Catholic priest from the Muslim area. That was the agreement. I think that everyone was in agreement, the HVO and the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: May we now take a look in this same document, the first sentence. It says: "Whereby SpanBat is granted pass after of its two APCs to supply Mostar hospital with plasma." Can we confirm that in this permission there are no figures mentioned with regard to the APCs or the crews of the APCs, no elements on the basis of which anybody would be able to identify which vehicles were concerned and which men manned those vehicles in crossing from one part of town to the other? Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's quite clear. It is said that two armoured vehicles are involved and the personnel, the usual personnel, plus the plasma. Two command staff, myself and somebody else, an interpreter, and an International Red Cross --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that. I do understand that. I'm just asking you whether you and I agree that this permission doesn't stipulate the actual persons or the number of vehicles, the number of APCs crossing. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does mention two vehicles, but it does not mention people.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to move on to another area, and that is the event that took place on the 11th of June, and I'm linking these two events up. It is the event in which Jesus Aguilar was killed. You said yesterday that a commission was established to investigate this case. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you know of any action on the part of this commission that was undertaken, and did you take part in the work of the commission at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not part of the investigating commission, and I know nothing about the results they arrived at. We were informed later in the command staff meetings general information, but I don't have first-hand information.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But I seem to remember you saying yesterday what the opinion of the commission -- of the commission was, and you even draw the conclusion that the commission completed its work and determined how the event had happened. Is that wrong? Today you say that you were just informed at the meeting of some general points and not of the details. So which of the two is correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think there's a contradiction here. I had general information about the work of the commission, to wit how Lieutenant Aguilar had been killed, from where the shot had come and where -- whether the person who had in fact killed lieutenant Aguilar had been investigated or questioned. And this is what we were told. The whole of the command staff were told. And this is what I said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm just going to ask you to take a look at some documents that are relevant to the work of this commission. May we first look about the daily information summary. It is 05111, Prosecution exhibit. And can we look at the date the 11th of June, please. Here we can see the last line where it says 11th of June, and you have it in Spanish. This daily information summary, you have it before you. Well, then, we can follow more easily. I will go through this rather quickly. We can establish, then, that on the 11th of June it says that during the transport of the medicines to the hospital officer Jesus Aguilar Fernandez was killed; is that correct? Let's look on the 12th of June. The 12th of June, line 3: "Meeting with minister of defence Stojic in Medjugorje in order to clarify the circumstances concerning the death of lieutenant Aguilar." Is that correct? And then on the same page we have the 13th of June, meeting in Mostar with deputy HVO minister Ivica Lucic and the commission for Lieutenant Aguilar in order to clarify the circumstances of his death. Is this correct? Very well. Well, then, please, let's look at the next page, the 15th and the 16th. The next page of this daily information summary. I don't see the 15th and the 16th. Oh, yes. Here it is now. Thank you. There's only one entry for the 15th: "Meeting between UNCIVPOL and the HVO [Realtime transcript read in error, "UN"] civil police in Medjugorje in order to consider the deaths of Lieutenant Aguilar." And then we have the 16th, line 3: "UN civilian police in Medjugorje took statements from the crew of Lieutenant Aguilar's vehicle." Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I haven't been able to find it. Yes. Yes, I can find it here now. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Then -- well, it's D, underneath D. Could we now have on e-court, P 02741.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think we ought to correct the transcript, because on page 21, line 12 and 13, lines 12 and 13, we read in English: "Meeting of UNCIVPOL and the UN civil police in Medjugorje." [Interpretation] Was that the civilian police of the United Nations or the HVO civil police? Because in the document in front of us, it says the civil police of the HVO, civilian police of the HVO. So which is it? I'd like some clarification. And may we have the document on e-court, please, the one we had a moment ago, with respect to the death of the Spanish lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You are quite right. I wasn't following the transcript. In the document of the 15th of June it says meeting between the UN civil police and the civil police of the HVO. Could we now see document P 02741. Dated the 13th of June. And in Spanish it's on page 2. The title is "Other activities." I don't see it in e-court. It should be on page 2, "Other activities." Yes, here it is. The date is the 13th of June, the date of the entire document, and it says: "At 1715 hours the minister of defence Stojic, the representatives of SpaBat held a meeting in the SpaBat headquarters in order to consider the circumstances of the incident where Lieutenant Aguilar was killed. It was decided that a joint commission should be established consisting of representatives of the HVO and the SpaBat in order to clarify all the circumstances. Later SpaBat asked the UN civil police for assistance so that the appropriate investigative actions have already been undertaken." Could you please have a look at another document, P 02761.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. What's the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By Your Honour's leave, I wish to look at all the information concerning this and then I will put my question at the end. The witness said he knew there was a commission. He knew that this commission worked, and he also said that he knows what the result was, that he knew the distance from which the shot came. He was able to identify approximately the building from which the shot was fired. So I would like to go step-by-step to reach the end result, and I will try to do so very quickly. P 02761. Is that the document we have before us? If it is, then in Spanish could the witness be shown page 2, "Other information."

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Page 2, underneath it says "Other information." The date is the 14th of June, 1993. "Other information," yes. It's at the bottom of the page. "At the second meeting with Minister Stojic in the SpaBat premises, it was decided to continue the investigation into the death of Lieutenant Aguilar. Leo Sorensen, the chief of UN civilian police will be in charge of the investigation. It was also agreed that an officer of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina will participate in the work of the investigation commission." Did you know that in fact the UN civilian police and Leo Sorensen who was in charge of it was the person appointed as the head of this investigation team?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I did not participate in the commission, I do not recall the name of the person in charge of the investigation. I was not there at the commission nor did I participate at the commission therefore I do not recall the name exactly. If this information happens to appear within a document from the higher command of the -- that that could very well be the case but I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Do you remember that the UN civilian police was involved in this investigation at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I seem to remember that, yes, that there were -- that they did participate. I commented these, that the commission had the support of the Spanish Battalion as well as the Croat forces. There was no inconvenience in investigating the death of the lieutenant. There were other two or three deaths and I cannot mix one investigation with the other, but I think that, yes, I believe that they investigated the death of Lieutenant Aguilar and that's what they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could we now have on e-court document 2D 00117. This is a document issued by the Defence department dated the 14th of June, 1993, and it's information provided by a member of the commission, Ivica Lucic, in connection with this event. As this information has been translated into English, for you sake I will read it out slowly to see whether it reflects the situation we have seen from the documents we have looked at. We do not have a translation into Spanish. On the -- the date is the 14th of June, 1993. It's issued by the Defence Department, and it says: "After the meeting of HVO representatives attended by head of Defence Department Bruno Stojic, head of Defence Department assistant Ivica Lucic and chief of military police Valentin Coric with the representatives of UNPROFOR Spanish Battalion, second in command Vice Colonel Castro and Major De Salas, it was agreed that head of Defence department assistant Lucic and Major De Salas will go to Dracevo where they were establish facts necessary for solving the case of lieutenant Fernandez's death: "On this occasion the following was established: "All damage to UNPROFOR vehicles was on the right-hand side. The gunshots came under an angle of at least 45 degrees to 90 degrees --" my attention was been drawn to the fact that in the transcript it says right. It should say left, was on the left-hand side. "... the gunshots came under an angle of at least 45 degrees to 90 degrees, and the nature of the damage to the armour these the shots were fired from a distance of about 50 metres, from a height of about ten metres. "Captain Fernando Alvares found a steel bullet mass which was 21 millimetres long, 6 millimetres wide, in a bag and tire of the transporter, which -- the carrier, which suggests a bullet of 7.62 by 51 calibre or 7.62 by 54 calibre. "Based on conversation with doctor Major De La Tores by analysing the autopsy results, we know that the entry wound had a diameter of 0.5 on the inside of the left shoulder blade, and the diameter of the exit wound was 1.5 on the right side of the neck." I know this is taking time, but as you cannot follow in English, I do have to read this to you. It says is that: "The bullet pierced the anti-armour vest, the bullet-proof west, the purpose of which was to protect against mortar shell fragments, broke multiple bones, two vertebrae and two shoulder blades, and on exit pierced two layers" -- my colleague has told me that the French translation is behind, so I'll wait a little. "... indicating a high initial velocity and kinetic energy, because the armour did not stop the spinning movement of the bullet. Based on the effects of the bullet, ricochet can be excluded and a firing distance of 50 metres at the most is implied. Taking into account the direction of the channel, it can be concluded that the bullet was fired from the height of a two-storey building, taking into consideration the height of the vehicle in which captain Fernandez was standing on the floor leaning to the left side." On the next page, page 2, it says that HVO positions were visited near the bank and the -- and the grammar school and that it was established that nobody was standing at salient or advanced positions. I'll skip over some parts. Because at those positions the -- the grammar school and the bank there is no optical view of the site of the event, and all this has been handed over for inspection to the representative of SpaBat, Major De Salas, and the UNPROFOR civilian police. I'll scoop over the passage which explains how the commission was established and who its members were, and then there's a passage which says "Major De Salas with our people visited our most advanced positions. He climbed up to places where our soldiers never go because it's too dangerous. He made video recordings, and he made sure that there is no possibility of shooting from these positions." And then we have a conclusion here made by Mr. Lucic, or, rather, he simply conveys the conclusion of the commission, which concluded that it was it the Muslim military that shot at the UNPROFOR vehicle from the position of the fourth primary school Revija and Hotel Bristol, and that Lieutenant Fernandez was shot from positions at Revija Hotel Bristol by a machine-gun with a calibre of 7.62 by 54 or an automatic rifle, 7.62 by 51. The commander of the Muslim forces is Semir Drljevic also known as Lovac or Hunter. Have you met this person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not recall having met this person.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: From this report, we can see there are some important differences from what you said yesterday. You were talking about the distance of the building from which shots -- the shots were allegedly fired. You spoke of a distance of 800 metres. So I wish to ask you now: On the basis of what you drew these conclusions yesterday. Was it on the basis of information you received from someone or was it your own conclusion? Because my understanding yesterday was that you yourself participated in the investigation when you spoke of the distance, the building, the angle of the shot. Where did you get all this information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I insist that I did not participate in the investigation, that I only was privy to the information that I received that emanated from the commission -- commission's investigation, which was composed of representatives from our high command and they reported to us on the conclusions arrived at by the commission as well as information given to us on the places or locations where the commission thought this shot would have come from, and the distance or the -- of the shooting and the calibre used of the particular weapon, and that's the information that I received to yesterday. And this information here, this report that you've just read is a document of the Croat defence forces, and I do not know whether they are trying to lay the blame on us or they're trying to exculpate themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... would like to ask. At what time did you get the information you have just spoken about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's very difficult to ascertain a precise time. On a daily basis we had continuous meetings, and every morning we had meetings as well as in the afternoons at different times of the day, and the following day after the death of the lieutenant we talked about the matter and we were receiving information on a constant updated basis. I cannot recall precisely what time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, Your Honours, I will round off this topic. I have two more documents to show before the break. Excuse me, Your Honour. I didn't see that you wished to put another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A technical question. The Defence has just told you that the lieutenant was hit by bullet that penetrated his left shoulder blade. The shot obviously came from the height unless he was standing askew at that point in time. According to the conclusions drawn, the armoured vehicle had bullet traces. They came from the left. These hits were from the left. The entrance point and the exit point of the bullet seems to demonstrate that the calibre used was 7.62. Machine-guns use bullets of such calibre. Other weapons do too, but given the conclusions of the autopsy and given the damage inflicted by the bullet according to what we've been told the kinetic force was such that the bullet must have been shot from a distance of about 50 metres and not from a distance of 800 metres. As an officer, you know that the velocity of a bullet diminishes with regard to the distance. The further away one is the less the velocity is. According to this document, the shot was fired at close range, and according to what we've been told, the bullet wasn't fired by the HVO but by the Muslim forces. So as a Spanish Battalion officer, what would your comment be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday, I also said, Your Honour, during one of the questions, I can't remember what question it was being asked of me, that every time at that something happened different parties would put the blame on the other party. And what I can see here in this document is that perhaps they're trying to lay the blame on the other party. In relation to the techniques of the weapons, the techniques of a sniper of the calibre of 7.62 has got sufficient force to cause the damage inflicted on the lieutenant. This perforated the bullet-proof vest twice on two occasions breaking the bones as mentioned there of the two vertebra. I do not know whether this was the weapon belonging to a sniper or a Kalashnikov that also uses a 7.62 calibre. If it is the weapon used by a sniper, I do not know exactly which weapon, but both can actually cause or inflict that sort of damage on the lieutenant. In relation to the impact caused on the APCs, on that date they were completely covered. They were -- they had been completely impacted upon. Every time they went through an area of conflict either the Tito Bridge or the demarcation line they were fired upon, therefore the impact of the gun as well as on the tyres, as well as on the actual cars themselves that was on a constant basis. Even the young lieutenants would often bet on who was the one to receive the most number of bullets. And I don't know if this technical answers your question, Your Honour. I would like to know perhaps if you have the report of UNCIVPOL, the civil police of the UN, who actually was responsible for the final report and to which I ascribe a lot more credibility. Not that I'm not attaching credibility to this, but this is what I would like to know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A while ago there was a document from the SpaBat, and it said that when the vehicle crossed the Tito Bridge there were fires that were shot. So we can imagine the scenario quite clearly. The vehicle was heading towards the bridge, crossing the bridge. The lieutenant was standing on the vehicle. There was a burst of fire which unfortunately resulted in the lieutenant's death. The burst of fire was opened from the left. So did it come from in front or from the left side. But technically speaking it seems that the burst of fire came from the left. It didn't come from behind or from in front or from the right. So what would you say from a technical point of view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] SpaBat carried out investigations of the place from which it is believed the shot was might both from one side and the other the way that the lieutenant was standing when the bridge was being crossed, he was not actually outside the armoured vehicle. He was actually crouching in it. He was crouching in it but his head was visible. So the shot actually crossed his back, went through the back and came out on the left-hand side. The bullet-proof vest, therefore, was crossed by the bullet and, according to the bullet-proof vest and how it was impacted by the bullet, it was clear that it was fired from the left-hand side. So we tried to locate precisely where that shot was fired from. There was a camera also that was taken to the place. A camera was attached to a -- the spot where we believe that the shot was fired from. A shot was fired from there and we believe this is exactly the place. There are pictures that we took that -- we took then of the zone, line of confrontation along the Mostar boulevard precisely taken at the place where we believe the sniper was hidden. And we can also see perfectly well from that place the Tito Bridge where the -- where the lieutenant was shot and killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It is implied in your last answer that you do not believe, you doubt that the description of findings read out by Ms. Nozica is correct. You are saying that they pretend facts which do not correspond to what the investigation of the Spanish Battalion found. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This report is dated three days after the death of the lieutenant. So they didn't really have time for a very thorough investigation, and I don't believe in the findings of this report. Personally, I do not attach credibility to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Just a minute. The subject is important that all the Judges have questions to put the witness. I'll give the floor to my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'd like follow up on a question put to you by Judge Trechsel, because you don't seem to have much faith in the investigation that was carried out jointly by the UN civilian police and the HVO civilian police. That's the report that we've been presented with by Defence counsel, Ms. Nozica. My question is as follows: On your side, was there another joint report compiled by the UN police together with the Spanish army or with the Muslim army? And my second question is: Is there a general joint report compiled by all the forces present, the purpose of which was to arrive at a conclusion that everyone could accept, a conclusion with regard to the death of the lieutenant we have been discussing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This report, if I -- my memory doesn't fail me, because of its heading it comes from the Croatian Defence Council. It is not a report from the investigating commission. I did not take part in the work of the commission but I do remember however that the investigating commission, the UN police always took part in it and there was a final report and I would imagine this final report, it does exist, it is filed somewhere. I'm sure it does exist I don't remember having seen it actually with my own eyes has I have never actually taken a look at this particular report of the Croatian Defence counsel either. The only information I had was such information as I got from one of my colleagues who was taking part in that investigating commission and that was the information he gave to the whole of the command staff. But I insist that this document stems from the Croatian Defence Council and not from the investigative commission. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, by your leave I have two documents but as they are in English it will take me some time to read it out, so I think it might be a good idea to have a break now for the sake of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll have our break now. It's 20 to 11.00, and we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now resume. Ms. Nozica, I've been informed that you have taken up 43 minutes so far, which means that you have some time left, but try to proceed rapidly. In theory, you have another two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have just as much time left as I have already used up, since that's the amount of time you granted me yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday, we granted you 45 minutes, and according to the calculations made, you have already used up 43 minutes. Yes. I do apologise. I have made an error. You have an hour and a half all together.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's really not a problem. Could we use the e-court to have 2D 00116 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: While this is being done, I would ask the following. You have heard the analysis of the HVO. Would you completely exclude the possibility that this bullet came from the side of the ABiH, the side of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Would you exclude such a possibility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe that the commission investigating the death of the lieutenant obviously does cover all possibilities. It would go into every single possibility, BiH or the HVO or indeed an accident or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. I still don't have document 2D 00116 on the screen. Could we scroll down to the first page. That's the previous document, 117.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, while we're looking for the document, you have present the documents that come from the HVO, but the Judges are asking themselves the following: The -- the UN conducted an investigation. Where are the conclusions of this investigation? You haven't found them or if investigation was conducted, conclusions must have been reached.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission this is something I will deal with very soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will wait in that case.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We have a letter here signed by Mr. Bruno Stojic. The date is the 14th of June, which is the same date as the date of the previous information we had a look at from Mr. Lucic. It is addressed to Julian Garcia Vargas, the Spanish minister of defence. Can you confirm that this gentleman was in fact the Spanish minister of defence at the time this letter was compiled? You have to answer because we cannot see. You are nodding in the transcript. It's a long letter so I won't read the entire letter out, but I would like to say that it contains all the elements that Mr. Lucic mentioned in his information. I would like to draw your attention to the part of the letter that concerns the minister. In the Croatian version it's on page 2. Just a minute. We'll find this in the translation too. In the translation it's page 0009. It says: "Minister," that's how it starts. It says: "Mr. Minister," Mr. Stojic is writing to the minister. "This case is completely clear to us and we are truly sorry about what has happened. We find it all the more regrettable that the fact that the death of lieutenant Fernandez is being used for political purposes and is the subject of manipulation. Your offices told us on the 12th of this month that you contacted them on two occasions and insisted that they accuse the HVO of murder, but being honourable men, they did not want to do this, and they did not want to draw any conclusions until an investigation had been conducted. We believe that the death of the late Fernandez was made good use of by someone to accuse the HVO without any grounds and to create a feeling of animosity on the part of the HVO towards the Spanish soldiers and to UNPROFOR in general, and to prevent UNPROFOR from fulfilling their tasks because of the failure of the BiH side to cooperate. "In order to inform the Spanish and international public of the truth, and in particular for the sake of Fernandez's family and for the sake of all the members of the Spanish army who were present in the area and still are in the area, today in Bosnia and Herzegovina for their sake we insist that a full investigation be completed and that the truth be determined by having recourse to any international and expert investigative commission that would act as an intermediary." And finally it says: "We want to maintain a correct relationship and good cooperation with members of the Spanish Battalion in this area. "Mr. Bruno Stojic." This letter was forwarded directly to SpaBat so that SpaBat could forward it to the minister of defence in Spain. Mr. Stojic never received a reply to this letter, and I would like to ask you whether you know anything at all about this letter and whether these elements have been mentioned, because there are certain accusations that concern the minister and his attempts to accuse the HVO, Croatia, and President Tudjman. Did you ever hear anything about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about the existence of this letter. I didn't even have a faintest idea the existence of this letter. I wasn't aware of it at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Now having put the ... [No interpretation] I would like to see the following document 2D 118 on the screen. It's an UNPROFOR document dated the 13th of July, 1993. It's from Mr. Sorensen, a letter from Mr. Sorensen, who was responsible for heading the commission. That's the correct document. It's also been signed. We can see the Croatian version on the other page. And since this letter is in English and it's not long, I'll read it out. You can see that the date is the 13th of July, and it's addressed to the Commissioner of the UN police. It's from Leo Bang Sorensen who is the commander of the Mostar police station. It concerns the death of Aguilar Fernandez Francisco and it concerns the Spanish Battalion in Mostar. The text is as follows: "With reference to the letter of the 16th of June, 1993, from Mr. Albert Benabou, it was agreed that the UN civil police would complete the internal investigation into the above-mentioned subject. "Following this agreement, the Spanish authorities, represented by Colonel Angel Morales Diaz-Otero and his legal advisor in conjunction with the HVO authorities, represented by minister -- the minister of defence of Herceg-Bosna Mr. Stojic, agreed that a special team from UN -- the UN civilian police would carry out an investigation on behalf of the Spanish authorities. It was also agreed that the HVO Civil Police would monitor the intern investigation on behalf of the Spanish authorities. "Part of the agreement states that having completed the investigation on both sides, Mr. Leo Bang Sorensen should consult with the chief of the HVO police, Mr. Filipovic, and the chief of the BiH police, Mr. Maslesa, with regard to their inquiries. "The UN civil police are not in a position to fulfil this commitment, due to the fact that the CIVPOL investigation team has been transferred outside of Mostar. "For your information. "Leo Bang Sorensen." Have you ever had the opportunity of seeing this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm afraid I was not aware of the existence of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. I think that this information from the president of the commission dated the 13th of July, 1993, is such that we can now conclude with this subject. I have one more question with regard to these events though. Do you know where the medicine came from, the medicine that was transported on that occasion? I think you mentioned something yesterday with regard to that subject can you remember what you said? Who sent that medicine to the eastern side of Mostar? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I remember that the medication left from the Croatian hospital of Mostar directed to the Muslim hospital of Mostar. The Croats demanded that there should be a TV crew accompanying the mission of delivery of the medication to the Muslim hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So the medical supplies came from the HVO hospital in western Mostar. Could we put it that way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. From a -- from a Croat -- from the Croat hospital towards the Muslim hospital. Indeed, yes, from the Croatian hospital to the Muslim hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. That's in fact what I said. That's fine. Yesterday, I think I understood you in a somewhat different way, and as a result I've prepared a number of documents that concern these medical supplies that were sent to the hospital in the eastern part of Mostar. It's from the assistant deputy of the Ministry of Defence, from the health department. Since we're moving on very slowly we'll try and deal with this at a later stage. Let's now move on to another subject. Have a look at document 1717, P 01717. It's -- it's a journal, an operative journal. We can have it on the e-court. 1717 is the number. The date, 16th of June. But first there's some questions I'd like to put to you, and the diary, the journal, mentions a number of events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The registrar has just pointed out to me that pursuant to Rule 70, document 1717 is a confidential one. Is that correct, Mr. Registrar? So if there is a question you would like to put to the witness, it should be done in private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you. Because I'll be using this document for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unless there are general questions you want to put to the witness without going into the details that might make it possible to obtain more precise knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll first put the question to the witness and we'll see.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Under the date, 16th of June, 1993, you have an event described which relates to the detention of a translator in the Konjic pocket. Do you remember this event? Did you participate in this event? Is there anything at all that you can tell us about this event?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do have a vague idea. What I read here is perhaps what I remember. There was a kidnapping of an interpreter in the Konjic pocket, but I didn't take part in that myself. It was the Jablanica detachment who took care of that and I personally have no specific memory of it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: That's quite enough for me, but could we just go through this document very briefly and establish what actually happened. If you see the date the 16th of June in the document -- well, we can go down to the send line where it says, "The representatives of the UNHCR, military monitors, went to the Konjic pocket to hold a meeting with the commander there. They did not request SpaBat escort, and at the end of the meeting a group of HVO soldiers threatened them with their weapons, fired into the air, detained their interpreters, and forced the representatives to leave. And they threaten them while doing so. It seems that the HVO personnel who detained the interpreters did so without the knowledge of the commander of the pocket who had met the representatives. They even threatened the HVO escort, the HVO escort that accompanied the representatives." And then the names of the interpreters are listed. And then it says: "Contact was established with the HVO in order to find a solution to the incident." You don't have the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]. I know the letter.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm not receiving any interpretation. I don't know what you said. Okay. Mr. Stojic is mentioned here, so let's please pay attention to this part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I believe you have not got interpretation so far, because actually you are -- you are speaking very fast. So please try to speak slowly, I would like to ask you, Madam Nozica, and also Witness BJ. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I wanted to look at the lower part of the document. It says: "Contact was established with the HVO in order to find a solution to the incident. At 1800 hours, two letters were received, one from General Lasic and another from the chief of the HVO Defence, Stojic, in which the command of the Konjic pocket was ordered to release the detainees. At 1845 hours, a platoon in the Jablanica detachment was ordered to take the letters and try to get the detainees released." Let's have a look at the next page because this event also transpired on the 17th of June, 1993. In the third line it says that: "Contact was established with the HVO headquarters so that they would order that the prisoners be released. They decided to send in Colonel Zarko Keza [phoen] to the Konjic pocket." And now at the end it says: "At 1300 hours, two telephones and INMARST was used." You must be familiar with that. That must be a special telephone line that you used. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Affirmative, yes. We know of the use of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So "those two telephone sets were put at the disposal of the commander of Konjic pocket and the HVO Defence Minister Stojic so that they could establish communication. Once this had been done, Zuric, who is the pocket commander, told the SpaBat unit commander that he would receive a reply at 1700 hours. So he would be told whether the detainees would be released or not." "At 1700 hours, he said that he would provide a reply at 1700 hours on the following day. "After intensive negotiations took place in the HVO headquarters and in the ABiH, and with the continual presence of the SpaBat platoon in the Konjic pocket, the interpreters and the driver who had been detained since the previous day by the HVO were released." As far as this event is concerned, there were several SpaBat reports. It was an interesting event which took place over a two-day period, so I'm not surprised you're familiar with the event. Since you know how things worked there at the time, could you tell us why you provided these two satellite phones on the 17th of June, 1993? Could one conclude that at that point in time Mr. Stojic did not have any phone contact with the Konjic pocket, with the area where these events took place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have refreshed my memory by reading the document, I recall more about it. And it's our opinion, we felt that the detention of interpreters aimed at being able to gain access to the HVO headquarters, and we put -- we made available these telephones in order for them to do so. But it wasn't I personally who made available these telephone lines. It was the Jablanica detachment that did so. And if I'm not mistaken, somebody said that an intelligence colonel also was allowed to enter the pocket in order to ease or to speed up the freeing of the interpreters. Once contact was established, the driver and interpreters were freed without any problems. Let me stress that always -- in such cases we always had cooperation from HVO and Mr. Stojic. We always did have their cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm very pleased to hear that, but what I'm interested in here is in two points, and they are these: First of all, let me tell you that Colonel Keza, from these documents we see that he did not reach those places because he was stopped by the BH army. Now, I don't have time to go through all the documents, but they are your reports and that's what it says in one of them. That's the first point. The second point is this: I repeat that this means that Mr. Stojic was not able to establish any other contacts without the satellite telephone that you supplied. And the second question: Doesn't it seem to you that Mr. Stojic was not a greet authority for those persons, because after he called up it was said that they would decide whether they would release them at all? And then they said, "We will decide that tomorrow." Then telephone conversations once again, and then only after those were they released.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is an opinion, but I always thought in the Konjic pocket -- that the Konjic pocket was not really, truly subordinate to military discipline as we understand military discipline in Western armies. And they did not follow HVO orders to the letter. They obeyed them more or less. They had moral authority, the HVO authorities in Mostar, of course, but the orders were not followed to the letter, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. And now finally I'd just like to just focus your attention to the question where you said that you had good cooperation with Mr. Stojic at all times. So I'd like to go back because I was saying to the question about Mr. Bozic. You said yesterday that you had extremely good cooperation with him and that when you succeeded in reaching him the problems that you had were mostly solved. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct to say that. It's correct to say that he was the best interlocutor we had to solve problems. Aside from that, I could tell you about all sorts of incidents in which he did not solve the problems and in which he himself caused a few problems, but it's anecdotal or isolated events.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And this is the last thing I want to ask you -- for that I need document 2D 00115 on e-court, please. Do you recognise this document or, rather, what's on our screens, what we're seeing in front of us? Do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's the coat of arms of the Canarias grouping. And it's a plaque, in which I cannot read what it says, but normally it's given as a souvenir to those who have cooperated or who have had links with us during our mission.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: May we zoom into the plaque? Well, I'll translate what it says on the plaque for him. It says: "To Mr. Bruno Stojic from the Spanish Battalion of UNPROFOR with gratitude." That's what it says on that little plaque there. And can I conclude precisely from what you said a few moments ago that Mr. Stojic was mostly the person who responded in positive fashion to your requests and that you had a good cooperation with him? Is -- was this the reason that he was granted this plaque of gratitude?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that it was the Canarias grouping, but, no, it wasn't the Canarias grouping. It was the Malaga grouping that gave this plaque to Mr. Stojic. But perhaps the Canarias group may have given a gratitude plaque. It's a tradition with us, the personnel who has cooperated with us or cooperates with us regularly and without any problem, is normally given as a plaque -- as a gift, as a souvenir, and this message or a message to that effect is in fact given. It's out of courtesy, out of politeness.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answers.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And thank you, Your Honours. That completes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one last question. I'd like to go back to the death of Lieutenant Aguilar. If I understood you correctly, an investigation was put in place to answer a number of questions, and in view of the document that the Defence showed you a moment ago, the mission left Mostar, UN mission left Mostar. Now, as far as you were concerned, was there no investigation when they left Mostar, or when they left Mostar did they continue their investigation? What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was surprised by the letter in which it was said that the civil police withdrew from the case. I had no knowledge of this. I was certain that the investigation had come to completion and that documents, final documents deriving from that investigation had been presented. So I was surprised by this letter of which I knew nothing. I was in fact convinced of the conclusions that I was basing my declarations -- on which I was basing my declarations this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that the death of colonel -- of Lieutenant Aguilar gave rise to a lot of emotion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, a great deal. It wasn't the first death in our group, so perhaps it was not such a shock as the first time we had a -- a deceased. But obviously the dead of a colleague was something shocking to our country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. We can continue. Who is next? Just a moment before I floor to the Defence counsel, I think that my colleague would like to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, may I go back to the death of Lieutenant Aguilar for a moment. It is rather troubling because we've just observed that the Trial Chamber did not know whether there was a report about this lieutenant, but if we go on to the next topic, we will have to know what the conclusions are of the UN police and the civilian police and their reports because the documents presented by the Defence, according to you, were not complete. So what should the Chamber conclude? Could you give us some more information? They don't seem to be reliable, you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Following the death of Lieutenant Munoz, the UN civil police did investigate because I was directly involved and I know that there was a final conclusion. I have not seen a document to that effect, but I take it that in the UNPROFOR archives or files you will find that. As for Lieutenant Aguilar's death and investigation, well, we were finally convinced, I cannot say we came to conclusions because there is no final document there are no conclusions; however, the Spanish Battalion was convinced as to the facts, and I was very surprised to see this letter from the Mostar civil police force saying that investigations are going to be stopped because they're not going to be in Mostar. I had no knowledge of this and I know not if there is a final report. These commissions work slowly, so perhaps work took a long time. But I cannot say any more. And it's true. I cannot say that these documents are fully reliable. I don't want to ascribe reliability just one side and therefore I cannot say that I can accept this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to complete the question posed by my colleague. You spoke about the death of lieutenant Munoz, and I'm looking at the transcript here. You said you were directly involved and that you learnt that there was a final conclusion.
