Now, this leads me to ask you the following question: In the indictment, which you don't have in front of you but I say -- I can tell that you in paragraph 115 it says that people beginning -- belonging to international organisations were killed or wounded on occasion, follow as a result of HVO fire. And then in the annex we have two victims, but there is no mention of Lieutenant Aguilar or Lieutenant Munoz. So the Chamber will have to make its conclusions based on paragraph 15. But you have just made a conclusion regarding Lieutenant Munoz. You said that you arrived at a final conclusion yourself. So what was this final conclusion? Who shot Lieutenant Munoz?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether a conclusion was reached, but listening to you, what you said is not what I said exactly. I said that an investigation did take place, that the civil police investigated the case. I was alongside the police force, the Norwegian police in this case, and when the investigation came to the end they took the results. I don't have the final conclusions. I never saw the final conclusions however I'm convinced as to what happened because I participated in the investigations but I never saw a document, a conclusion document. And allow me to remind you, because I think it is necessary to recall that we had another -- another casualty in our grouping in the Canarias task force due to a mortar shot in Jablanica, a legionnaire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you're saying as far as Lieutenant Munoz is concerned, you had no knowledge of a final investigation and conclusion conducted by the people who were in charge of the investigation. That is to say the Norwegian police. That's what I can see on the transcript on page 48, line 5 where you said this. So you cannot in fact tell us where the shot came from, whether it was a shot from the Serbs, the Muslims, or the HVO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, of course lacking the final conclusions or results I cannot so say. I am convinced about something but that's what it is. It's something I'm convinced about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what are you convinced of what? What are you convinced of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm certain that it was a mortar shell from the Mount Hum locations and that they knew perfectly well that the ones in the area at that time were Blue Helmets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're telling us that it was a shell from Mount Hum.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Hum is the mount's name. H-u-m, Hum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, on to the next Defence team. Mr. Praljak's Defence counsel. You have two hours and 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Good afternoon, Your Honours. On behalf of General Praljak, a brief cross-examination conducted by myself, after which General Praljak, in keeping with the guidelines you gave him last time, will be asking the witness some questions which are solely of a technical and military nature.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to you, Witness. My name is Nika Pinter attorney from Zagreb, and together with Mr. Kovacic we represent General Praljak's Defence. As I've already said, I -- my cross-examination will be brief, just two short questions, and then General Praljak will be asking you questions about the events that took place almost 13 years ago, and I'd like to ask you to do your best to remember those events and answer the questions to the best of your recollections. Yesterday, my colleague of the Prosecution asked you, and this was in June when you discussed your arrival to Herzegovina and Mostar, he asked you about your meeting with General Praljak or, rather, he asked you about General Praljak, and you mentioned that you had heard of General Praljak and that you knew that he was a member of the Croatian army. Now, that part of your answer came when we were discussing letting through the ambulance taking a wounded member of your group, transporting a wounded member of your group. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that when we talked about the injured, that is to say Lieutenant Munoz, and we were allowed to go through because General Praljak was, as it happens, around there then, it was said that he was a member of the HV army, and I believe there were photos of him in his uniform with the insignia which so attests.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: When you did see that photograph of him with a uniform with insignia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember well, I met General Praljak in a meeting at Medjugorje, and I could say that it was just the day before what happened to Lieutenant Munoz, and, if not, a day later in a Croat paper there was an interview published and the photos accompanying the article were included in our reports. We stated that he was wearing the HV army insignias or badges.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, tell me if you know why on the 11th of May General Praljak was in Mostar in the first place. You don't know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know not. He may well answer, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Fine. Do you know that General Praljak was born in Grabovina, Capljina municipality, which is in Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did know this because of his personal history file which we had.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: If you had his CV at your disposal, then I'm sure you know that General Praljak, throughout your mandate there, the time you spent in the territory of Herzegovina, was not a member of the Croatian army. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had information that he was. I don't know whether it was correct or not, but our information stated that he belonged to the Croat army before he came chief in the Serbo-Croat army. I don't know whether this information was correct or not, but I'm not mistaken, that was the information we had.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: I don't know whether there's been a mistake in the translation or whether the witness said something different, but let me ask you this way: Was it a Serbo-Croatian army? Because in the transcript it says, "I don't know whether it was correct or not, but our information stated that he belonged to the Croat army before he became chief of the Serbo-Croat army." That cannot be correct.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe I said Serbo-Croat, but I meant to say Bosno-Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, may we have on e-court the following document, 3D 00363. It's a set of documents that I'm going to show you which relate to the relieving of duty and appointing of General Praljak --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you provided us with a set of documents? MS. PINTER [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ah, yes. It was the registrar that forgot to hand it to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, for once the registrar got it wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour the documents were also handed over to the Spanish booth, so this will facilitate interpretation. The document is 3D 00363.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: It will come up on your screen but the interpreters will interpret as well. I do apologise. I seem to have made a mistake myself. That's not the right document. The document is 3D 00278. 3D 00278. Never mind. It's not on our screens yet, but let's not waste our valuable time. It is a decision by the personnel department of the Ministry of Defence, and the date is the 15th of June, 1993, and as of that date the military service of Slobodan Praljak terminated in the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia. Major General Slobodan Praljak on the 1st of June tabled a request to go to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Have you received the translated document or, rather, have you received the interpretation of it? Was that customary -- is it customary procedure in the army to issue a decision terminating active military service? Do you know this as a general rule, as a general practice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about the Croat army. No. I mean, one has to request a leave, and until the leave is granted declaration of intent is not enough. One has to receive it in writing.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Yes, but the decision made by the Ministry of Defence by which somebody's active military service ceases is a different matter. Does that mean that he ceased to become a people of the Croatian army at that point in time when this decision was made and issued?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Just a moment. I apologise. Give you some time. Yes, document 3D 00280 next, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm turning to the Defence with regard to this document, which states that Mr. Praljak was leaving the Croatian army as of the 1st of June, 1993. If you're going to tender this -- want to tender this into evidence, then what the Judges want to know is article -- and in service in the armed forces which results in the text that appeared in the Official Gazette, 5291. That would allow us to look at the regularities, whether this was regular practice or not. You'll have time to do that between now and later on. Perhaps after the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we will hand in that rule. Your Honour, I'd just like to tell you that this decision of the 15th of June was written on the 15th of June, and General Praljak's request was made on the 1st of June. So that is 3D 00310.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd just like to note for the record what the document says, at least in the English translation, is not that Mr. Praljak left the Croatian army but he was released from active service in the Croatian army. I think that is an important difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may respond, Your Honours. We shall adduce a series of documents that will clearly show this. However, I believe this document speaks for itself because it says that Slobodan Praljak's active duty military service has been terminated, and at that point he ceased to be active member or indeed a member of the Croatian army. The date is the 15th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Witness, you have before you a document which is entitled "Request," or "Application," we preceded the issuing of the decision.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is how it appears in the French language and I do have a copy here.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Very well. After General Praljak was no longer an active-duty member of the Croatian army, he was appointed commander of the HVO Main Staff by a decree of President Mate Boban. And could we please have document 3D 00279 on e-court. The date is the 24th of July, 1993. I hope you see it on the screen. On the 24th of July, we can say that General Praljak became the commander of the HVO Main Staff. Do you agree with this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document appears in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: You haven't received it in Spanish?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: However, can you hear the interpreters translating it into Spanish? Because we have provided a copy to the interpreters. I will read this out to be on the safe side. "Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Croatian Defence Council, Defence Department Main Staff, 24 July, 1993." I won't read out the number. "Notification for all HVO units. "We hereby inform all HVO HZ HB units," that means the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, "that pursuant to the decree of the president of the HZ HB, Mr. Mate Boban, Major General Slobodan Praljak is appointed to the post of commander of the HVO Main Staff. "This notification is to be communicated to the lower levels of command." The date is the 24th of July. Do you agree with me that as of the 24th of July Slobodan Praljak became the commander of the HVO Main Staff? You left the territory of Herzegovina after the 23rd of September when the last report was lodged by your group in September, 1993, but I will put a question to you to round off this series of questions. Do you know when Slobodan Praljak was the commander of the HVO Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not know. We knew already when he had been appointed to the -- as commander of the HVO Main Staff, but I do not recall the date. After I left Bosnia-Herzegovina, I left contact -- I lost contact and I did not receive much information after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: You did not receive information about what was happening in the area after your departure?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Once my mission had terminated in Bosnia, I did not officially receive any further information. In relation to the information that I had received, the task force that came after the Canarias task force was task force of parachutists that I was familiar with. That was the only information I could have received but not official information.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Therefore, you could not discuss the contents of any documents issued after you left Bosnia-Herzegovina? After September, 1993, that is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, reports were never discussed. Either they're received or they're not received. And on a general basis we did receive information as to what the situation of operations was there in a general sense, but never on a particular basis in terms of what the operations were like.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have one more document. 3D 00280. It's a document whereby Major General Slobodan Praljak is discharged from his duty at a his request on the 8th of November, 1993. We will now move on to another topic, after which I will give the floor to Mr. Praljak. Yesterday, we saw some footage from Spanish television showing the stopping of the convoy in Citluk, the convoy which on the 25th of August was supposed to enter eastern Mostar, and you were present on that occasion escorting the convoy. You said that the convoy was stopped. Could you please confirm that the convoy was stopped by refugees?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Before we go on to that, I just wanted to -- I was checking the transcript to make sure that there was no question. The last exhibit was shown to the witness with no question. It was simply put forward to the Chamber. I just want to indicate the Prosecution does not dispute the date that Mr. Praljak left as commander of the HVO. It was on approximately the 8th or 9th of November. It's not disputed. It's in the indictment, exactly that date. However, we do not accept that it was as a result of illness, and that will be a disputed point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Ms. Pinter, you mentioned document 280, according to which Major General Praljak was relieved of his command as a result of medical problems, and it was effective as of the 8th of November, 1993. The witness should then be asked the following question: Although he had left earlier on, was he familiar with the fact that General Praljak had been relieved of his command? And this would have made it possible to establish a link between the document, your question, and the witness. And then you could take advantage of this by asking him whether he was aware of the fact that General Praljak was ill. He would then say, "Yes, I did," or, "No, I didn't," because quite rightly the Prosecution has pointed out that you refer to a document and then you move on to another subject.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Before showing the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, please. There's something that Judge Prandler would like to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: A follow-up question I would like to ask from you, Ms. Pinter, concerning the issue when we have here two documents. The first one which you just referred to, that is the document 3D 00280, which -- in which Major General Slobodan Praljak was relieved of his duty at his own request. It was signed by Mate Boban, about which we are now talking. But at the same time, if you compare with another document in the same file, it is number 00695991, and it is about a -- in French, "Demand," in English, "Application." It was dated as a matter of fact on 20th of October, 1993, in Medjugorje, and in this General Praljak asked the following in his application to the ministry of defence of the Republic of Croatia, and in the second paragraph of that application it says: "I am filing this application for readmittance to the minister of defence of the ministry of defence of Croatia with the hope that my application will be approved." "With the hope that my application will be approved." Frankly, my question is if he asked to be released from the Main Staff at his own request in October of 1993 as a result of his illness, I do not see the logical line that at the same time that even of 10 days ago of that request, he requested the Croatian Ministry of Defence to be readmitted to the Ministry of Defence in Croatia. So I wonder, Ms. Pinter, if you would be good enough to explain what are the connections between the two requests. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this will be much better explained by Mr. Praljak himself when he rises to his feet, because he's familiar with the procedure and why he had to write this on the 20th of October, because proceedings take time. The procedure takes time. But General Praljak will explain it better himself. All I can say is the following: General Praljak submitted a request to be released from the HVO, and at the same time he asked to be admitted into the Croatian army. As all this involves certain procedures, there are different dates on the documents. What we wished to show was that after he left the HVO in November, 1993, General Praljak asked to be taken back into the Croatian army but not so that he could be an active-duty soldier, rather that he could return to the Ministry of Defence where he had a job which was less demanding and less fatiguing than the work he was doing in the HVO since his health no longer permitted him to continue with that work. I began asking something about the convoy stopped in Citluk on the 25th of August, and I asked if you would agree with me whether it was refugees from Bosnia who stopped the convoy and there were some attempts to let the convoy pass through, but that it was stopped in Citluk for some four hours; is this correct.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Affirmative, yes. There were refugees, civilian personnel who surrounded the APCs and they actually stood in front of the APCs and they detain the convoys for a period of two or three hours, perhaps four hours. I'm not going to argue that but approximately two or three hours from my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Yes, we agree with that. And it was only after General Praljak arrived that the convoy was able to pass. I will now show you some video footage, and I will ask you to take a look at it, after which I will put one or two more questions to you and that will be the end of my part of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, to continue what Mr. Mundis was saying last week, there's a number of items that are not in dispute. The Prosecution does not dispute for one moment that Mr. Praljak was involved in allowing the convoy to proceed through Citluk, that he intervened. We've seen this video before. He was also shown in the video the Prosecution showed yesterday very briefly, and there is absolutely no dispute about this whatsoever. I don't see any reason to show the video yet again in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Pinter, if you want to show the video it means that you have a certain reason to do so, there is something you want to add to what we have already seen. Mr. Praljak is raising his hand to say that he doesn't agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He doesn't agree but it's very short footage, less than a minute, and I do have a reason for wanting to show it. The Prosecutor left it out yesterday deliberately.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going have to object to that part. It's on the tape. I saw it myself. Mr. Praljak is on the tape, and we can play it again if that's necessary. So I object to that characterisation by counsel that we deliberately left it out. I'll ask that we play the tape again to show that that's absolutely not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll have a look at the video. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] This is not about love. I have eight trucks here. They have to be taken to the Croatian people in Vitez and Vares. Eight dead bodies have to be brought from Mostar. This is not about love. The convoy has been inspected. We have to save people, the people up there. What has happened has happened. The army will do its job. To feed the Croats in Vares, in Zepce, in Vitez, we have to let this through. There's no discussion about it. Let's go."

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's enough. Before putting a question to the witness, I just wanted to check whether Your Honours have received the transcript of this video and whether it's in your files. Otherwise, I will have to say something about the text. The video is 3D 00366 for the record and for purposes of checking.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: I'll just put one question to you after this video. Does this correspond to the situation you remember as you remember it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Affirmative, yes. That was the case. It reflects exactly what took place there in Citluk.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: It's a fact that General Praljak solved this not in a military way but in an instinctive and humane way. Would we agree? This was not done by military methods. Before him there were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I don't understand the question. What would be a military method as opposed to what was done here? I don't understand the question, Your Honour. Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, a question has been put to you. We just watched a video, and the Judges noted that there were a number of UN armoured vehicles, the passage of which had been obstructed by civilian population, and they did not seem very happy. We also saw some wooden obstructions, et cetera. So we saw an individual who climbed up onto the first vehicle. He was wearing a military uniform but had no insignia on him. So in fact one could say we don't really know who climbed onto the vehicle. And then we heard this individual give a sort of humanitarian speech. He said there are Croats in certain places that need to be provided with food, that the crowd was obviously not happy. They did not agree. And then this individual said, "We have to move on." And then the first vehicle started moving forward and the obstruction was removed. These images are very strong images. We see that the UN had been obstructed and one sole individual made it possible for the convoy to move on. So when you see such images, as an officer, would you say that the operation concerned is a military one or would you say, as was implied in the question put to you, that a member of the military tried to convince those obstructing the vehicles that certain humanitarian considerations should be given weight and the convoy should be let through? As a member of the Spanish Battalion, what sort of conclusions would you draw from all of this? Naturally, as Judges, we are quite capable of assessing the nature of the situation, but as you were a high-ranking officer in the Spanish Battalion, what sort of conclusions would you yourself arrive at? Having said that, naturally the Judges have their own conclusions that may or may not agree with the ones that you can draw from the images shown.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, because we seem to have a problem. Fine now. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That particular APC where General Praljak got on top, I was -- happened to be there, but I do not get shown on the video. It was the first truck, the first APC, part of a convoy. It was a very difficult time. It was becoming more and more violent as time went by, and I recall that one of the ministers of Croatia, he was there with the refugees, tried to convince the crowds that we could be let through. He did not manage to achieve this, and General Praljak, in a sign of authority, he arrived. He got on top of the APC. He addressed the crowds, and he managed to persuade them. And of course we did not use any military methods. He did not send any soldiers to let the vehicles through, but with his voice and his authority he managed to achieve what we were after, which was to be able to be let through with the convoy. And having spoken to the crowds he managed to achieve this and we were let through. And I recall this incident because it was an act in which it wasn't a very easy moment for us and they managed to be let through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Did you also give a medal for good cooperation to General Praljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, there is a saying in Spanish that says, well, "If -- if you are born and with good manners, you will be greeted accordingly." And I'd like to mention this in relation to that as a way of answer to your question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we have understood you correctly, you're saying that it is Mr. Praljak's intervention that made it possible for the convoy to move and to accomplish its mission, because Mr. Praljak addressed the crowd and told them that it was necessary for them to bear in mind certain humanitarian considerations, not to think of military objectives, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time I heard that, even though the interpreter was next to me, the interpreter did not interpret that. I never managed to understand what he said. Now I'm able to understand. At the time I did not understand what he was saying. I knew that he was speaking in Croatian language and that he managed to convince or persuade the crowds to let us through. At the time I did not understand what he was saying in that language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Pinter, we have a few more minutes until the break.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have completed my part of the cross-examination. Now the general will continue, but I wanted to answer the question concerning the document where it appears I did not put a question to the witness about the document. Actually, before I show the document, I asked the witness when he left Bosnia-Herzegovina and his mission, and whether he knew that the general was relieved of his duty, and that is why I felt I could show the document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is 12.30. We'll now have our 20-minute technical break and we will resume at ten to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll now resume. We have 45 minutes left, and I'd like to remind Mr. Praljak that he has permission to put technical questions to the witness, but he should avoid making comments, declarations, or he should also avoid declaring his innocence. So as a high-ranking officer, you may put technical questions to another high-ranking officer. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, although I don't remember ever having said that I was innocent. I don't remember ever having addressed that problem in such a manner.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Witness. Since time is short as usual, I would be grateful if you could provide concise answers to my questions, say, "I know," "I don't know," or "I can't remember," and this will make it possible for me to get through all the questions that I think I should put to you and that might help us clarify certain matters. Thank you very much. Let's continue with the subject of the convoys on the 20th. On the 21st, a convoy of 16 vehicles passed through, and then a few days later there was a second convoy, a 300-tonne convoy providing food and medical supplies for the other side. My first question is as follows. Do you know that the food and medical supplies were intended both for the civilian population and members of the military on the left side of the river?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that was the case indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: According to your testimony, didn't you say I was on the first vehicle and remained there for the first 30 kilometres right up until entry into Mostar, and this was seen in the film, in the video shown by the Prosecution yesterday. Was that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it was my APC, but I don't know whether it was 30 kilometres or 20 kilometres. We went all the way down to the Mostar valley. That's all I can remember.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you accept my explanation that that was because of -- in the fear that some fool might obstruct the convoy on that road once again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I understand that you didn't want any problems with that convoy until it had completely left the city of Citluk and it was already well on the road to Mostar, yes. I understand that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that prior to that event, and this is what you have said yourself, the minister of the foreign affairs of the Republic of Croatia Mate Granic addressed the same people, the same crowd, and then-president of the HVO government Mr. Jadranko Prlic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I remember the Croatian minister. I didn't know he was the foreign affairs minister. I thought he was the minister in charge of refugees. But I do remember him. I don't remember Mr. Prlic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: In a lengthy excerpt that concerned the same event certain things could be seen, and my question is as follows: In such a war, the war that you yourself experienced, the difference between what one wants and what one can actually realise in the field was often considerable.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, couldn't hear the translation at all.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... receiving any translation, any interpretation. It's fine now.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: In that war, do you often notice that there was a great difference between what one wanted to do and what one was actually able to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I object to the question, Your Honour. Who? Are we talking about people on the HVO side? Are we talking about the Spanish Battalion? I think it's sheer speculation to ask this witness questions like that unless there's further foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you want to put this question to the witness for what purpose? What event does it concern?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It concerns Mr. Granic and Mr. Prlic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: The goodwill existed, but the possibility of actually doing what one wanted to do was a different matter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I still object, Your Honour. There's no foundation that this witness has any idea of what Mr. Prlic or Mr. Granic intended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, we fail to understand the purpose of your question. You have just said that Mr. Granic, the minister of foreign of affairs of Croatia intervened, but his intervention didn't bear any fruit. Similarly, Mr. Prlic intervened with the crowd but obtained no results, and then you intervened and that had results. Are you trying to demonstrate what your role was in comparison with the role of the other two mentioned what are you trying to demonstrate to the witness. The Prosecution says there is no foundation for such a question. The Judges also wonder about the matter. We're trying to see things clearly ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to add a more technical comment. The fact that not only in war but in life we often cannot by far achieve what we want to achieve is so common that it must not be proven. It falls under article -- under Rule 94(A), really. It's not something that we can take evidence on. It's common knowledge.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll move on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: After the convoy had entered Mostar, yesterday we saw when watching the video that there was 105-millimetre howitzer on the Muslim side. We also saw some soldiers. Could you tell me how many artillery weapons the ABiH had on the left bank of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Artillery, I didn't see anything. I did see mortars but no artillery weapons, none whatsoever. It doesn't mean that they weren't there. I personally didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell me, in the Marsala Tita Street, which you drove down, it seemed very damaged. It's a street that you had passed through before the conflict between the ABiH and the HVO. Was that street, was that road in such a damaged situation even prior to the beginning of the conflict in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many damaged areas. Not as much and as intensely as afterwards, but there were already many damaged areas.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Prior to the conflict between the ABiH and the HVO in Mostar, the conflict that started on the 9th of May, 1993, prior to the conflict, whenever you went to eastern Mostar, did you notice even a single mosque that hadn't been either damaged or completely destroyed?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't get -- I didn't get the translation. I don't know if there was an answer or not but -- sorry. I again object to the question unless there's foundation for how much this witness spent in Mostar prior to the 9th of May. The testimony is that he arrived on the 19th of April only about two weeks or so before this happened. There's been no testimony that he was in fact in Mostar prior to the 9th of May, and before he's allowed to answer that question I think some foundation should be laid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may to respond. [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may respond to that. The problem is that the Prosecutor is also using documents that concern a period prior to the arrival of this witness and documents that concern the period after the witness's departure. That can be seen in the list of documents. The documents will probably be part of this testimony, so we should make a decision about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Praljak is putting a question to you. It interests me. I don't know whether my colleagues are interested in this question. Yes, apparently that is the case. Prior to the 9th of May -- you arrived there in April, but between April and May did you ever move around Mostar? Did you have the opportunity of examining the streets, the churches, the mosques? Were you in Mostar prior to the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Affirmative, yes. I was in Mostar. I did take a walk on the streets, and I went into the shops. I went to the Muslim area. No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Praljak put a question to you just a minute ago prior to the 9th of May. Could you see with your own eyes buildings that had been damaged or destroyed? I am putting a general question to you. Prior to the 9th of May, did you see any buildings in the town that had been damaged by various projectiles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the whole area where we were there was a great deal of damage. Practically every single bridge was down and there were many constructions, houses probably, mostly houses destroyed. We thought it was from the previous Serbo-Croatian war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the previous war I'll conclude and then give the floor to my colleagues. Mr. Praljak also mentioned a mosque. Prior to the 9th of May did you see any mosques that had been destroyed, partially destroyed, damaged? Did you yourself see this with your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't recall that. I can't say there wasn't or that there was one but I can't recall personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Actually, the question was put in negative terms, whether you had seen any mosque which was completely intact, not damaged or destroyed. Do you recall having seen any mosque that looked okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so. Yes, I think there were totally undamaged mosques. At least the minarets looked perfectly undamaged.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: On the left or the right bank of the Neretva River?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the left. When I say the left, I mean East Mostar, Muslim Mostar.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could we now place a document on the ELMO, please. The number is 3D 00369. The date is the 31st of July, six days after I was made commander of the Main Staff. And the order --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can't see the document on the screen because it hasn't been correctly placed on the ELMO. Could Madam Usher please sort the problem out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, there seems to be some confusion. The document which the lady just putting on the ELMO, it is in the e-court so we can get it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It doesn't matter. We can see it now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I'll read it out, and I would be grateful if it could be interpreted, translated. Under number 1: "I order members of the HVO officers and the ranking officers in the zone of responsibility, the following: Commanders in the command on all levels have no right to stop, control, or search UNPROFOR weeks." Under item 2: UNPROFOR units should be allowed to move around freely, and they are to be offered full protection and are to be guaranteed -- they are to be guaranteed free movement in the previously approved directions and routes that will be promptly submitted to you." Under 3: "Humanitarian aid convoys are not to be permitted to pass through without having fully inspected their loads. After the convoys have been searched, they shall be allowed to move on in the previously approved directions under escort and with occasional controls." Were you familiar in any way with this order of mine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of this one at all. This one specifically I was not aware of.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Under item 3, or with respect to item 3, were you aware of the fact that humanitarian aid convoys were used to transport a lot of medical supplies that were no longer valid? Their expiry dates had already been reached. Are you aware of fact that such convoys were used to -- to transport goods intended for sale on the black market? They used such convoys for trafficking in goods. Are you aware of the fact that one often received information according to which such convoys were used to transport high-risk waste from certain chemical factories located in some of the countries that donated this aid?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no idea of any of these things that you have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Although you left the area, did you learn from the newspapers or in some other way that 136 tonnes of medical supplies remained in the Mostar hospital, and these medical supplies had been produced in 1951 or 1952, et cetera, and it had been -- they had been provided -- these medical supplies had been provided as humanitarian aid in these convoys?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object again; witness has already testified earlier today that he did not keep himself -- stay informed, or follow developments in the area after he left at the end of September. We're just wasting time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But when your convoys transported humanitarian aid, and in particular medical supplies, did SpaBat officers examine the contents of the convoys, the loads transported? I don't know where Mr. Praljak obtained this information, but he is saying that medical supplies produced in 1951 and 1952 were discovered in a Mostar hospital. So they were over 40 years old, and they can't have been valid. So did you examine such goods?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to correct something. He didn't say medicine, he said medical supplies. That could include bandages or other items that one does not consume. It could also include objects that although very old can be used. Perhaps it would be better if Mr. Praljak could be more precise to the information or the origin of this information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could Mr. Praljak also mention the high-risk or toxic waste that he has referred to. In which country did it come from? Because we're now confusing humanitarian aid and invalid medicine, all sorts of products.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Praljak, please be more precise when putting your question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: In the humanitarian aid convoys -- my question concerns these humanitarian aid convoys. You can either say -- agree with me or not. But in these convoys, there were a lot of -- there was a lot of medicine over 40 years old, and such medicine couldn't be used. And I'm mentioning this because the hospital in Mostar, after the end of the war, had to burn 136 tonnes of such medicine. I wasn't referring to any other medical supplies. I was referring to a lot of smuggled goods that were smuggled by using these humanitarian convoys. My question was whether you are aware of the fact that weapons were also smuggled through in such convoys together with food or tinned food and such weapons were produced in the territory of Croatia. We'll mention this later on. And I also mentioned other information we had. I want to know whether you had such information, information according to which certain people wanted to use those convoys to transport toxic waste to the salt mine in Tuzla or other places on the way there. We knew about that, and this is why, as can be seen in item 3, we had to control such convoys. We had to examine such convoys, to make sure that Bosnia and Herzegovina didn't become a territory where waste would be left, because a lot of money was spent on such things. My question is --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whether you had knowledge of any such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... what Mr. Mundis has said last and we've said earlier. Can we understand now that Mr. Praljak is giving evidence? He's making declarations of fact in court and then this is evidence that the Prosecution can use against him in the future? He is giving --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Mr. Scott, that's not quite right. Mr. Praljak says that he issued an order, and in paragraph 3 it says that humanitarian aid convoys shall be permitted to pass only after having been examined, and he is asking the witness whether he was aware of fact whether there were humanitarian convoys that were transporting either medicine or -- that was no longer valid or toxic waste or weapons. Toxic waste would be transported to Tuzla or they would transport other good, they would smuggle other goods. So this question relates to a document that he himself signed, and he is asking the witness what his opinion is, because the accused is saying that in paragraph 3 of this document it says that humanitarian convoys should be controlled because there were rumours according to which arms were being smuggled through in this way. And he mentioned a hospital in Mostar in which faulty medicine had to be burnt. The witness will just have to answer by saying, "I don't know anything about that, or yes that's correct or that's not correct." Your objection is just wasting time. The Judges would like to know whether the accused's allegations are true or not. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I most respectfully disagree. The document itself says nothing about any of these things. It is simply Mr. Praljak on his feet making factual assertions in the courtroom and asking this witness, if he speculates, to agree with him. There is nothing in the document that says anything about toxic waste or about weapons or about medicines being over 40 years old. There's nothing in the document. The only thing we have in the courtroom is Mr. Praljak getting up and making factual assertions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, if I may be heard just very briefly and I don't mean to interrupt General Praljak's cross, but there is one document, P 02286, generated by -- or having come through this particular gentleman, and there is a reference at least in the document itself on page 6, I'll just read it very quickly. It says: "This has led to reinstatement of escort for convoys throughout the whole journey, and on one occasion BH command asked the Spanish Battalion to check the loads on the lorries in Metkovic to guarantee that there was no repeat of the incident last month when a shipment of ammunition was found in a UNHCR lorry." This is a document generated by this gentleman's organisation. Clearly there had been at least one incident where ammunition was found being transported by the UNHCR, well, in one of their lorries, and so it would appear that this would justify the line of questioning that General Praljak is asking. And I also want to mention that these are documents that we received from the Prosecution. So obviously they are aware of this incident, and I'm rather disappointed at the objection being raised by Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I consider, and you mentioned this as well, although I don't know whether it's clear to everyone in court, Mr. Praljak is asking these questions relevant to the document being shown. So he -- here a search of the trucks is called for. Now, the reasons can be justified or unjustified. So he's asking why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Witness, did you have knowledge of an incident by which an UNHCR convoy contained any weapons? So the answer can either be yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. My second question: We have just seen that there's an order asking the HVO to check humanitarian convoys. Now, you in SpaBat, did you know that the HVO wanted to visit humanitarian convoys and search them? Yes or no once again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, President, but my answer can only be the same one. All parties said and alleged that humanitarian convoys were also being used to transport ammunition, to smuggle goods. It is something that they repeated continually, ever since I arrived in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Praljak, we have ten more minutes, because after ten minutes we're going to conclude the cross-examination which will continue tomorrow because Mr. Karnavas would like to deal with some matters till quarter to 2.00. So you have ten minutes left, and we'll continue with the cross-examination tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Sir, when you were on the eastern side of Mostar, east bank, in Marsal Tito Street, in the houses together with the inhabitants and population, was the 4th Corps command put up there as well as the military police of the BH army? Were they located there too? And the command of the Mostar Brigade of the BH army? Were they located and put up in the town itself, mixed amongst the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The general headquarters of the armija, was it mixed up with the civilian population? I do think so. They were, in fact, housed in a house that was surrounded by civilian houses. I'm not sure whether that is your question, however.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, that's the answer to my question, but in another building was there the headquarters of the Mostar Brigade of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in the third building the headquarters of the military police of the BH army, the 4th Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The general headquarters were there. But I would have to see an actual map of the area to see exactly where they were located, but yes, they were in the area.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the usher now place two documents -- or, rather, hand two documents to the witness, put them on the ELMO. Would Madam Usher put these two documents on the ELMO, please. 3D 000345 of the number of the first document. And so we have 3D 000345 is the first document. This one here. Madam Usher, would you take this document, please. Madam Usher, would you take this document from me and put it on the ELMO here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Sir, I have marked south here, south, east, and at the bottom I put North Camp, which was previously used by the Yugoslav People's Army. So I've marked North Camp. And I've also marked where the railway station in Mostar is, that is to say in the northern district of Mostar. The black dots, four black dots shows the compound that was called and referred to as North Camp, the area it covered. It's a large area. It takes up almost a quarter of the whole area of the town. Do you know about the existence of North Camp under the control of the BH army on the left bank? After the 30th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot pinpoint the place you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I have marked it with dots. But as it's black and white, I can't find the dots now. It is the Neretva River, the left-hand corner where the road joins the river, meets the river, right down until you get to the bridge, this bridge across the Neretva River. Almost at the bridge itself, not quite. So go right, please, right along the road, take your pointer right along the road, towards the south, move southwards, along the road, that's right, just keep going straight, straight, straight, straight, pointing to the road until a point that I'm -- stop. Then towards the Neretva River. Down towards the river. Straight down towards the river. And now that is the border. The Neretva River is the border. So it was at the entry into Mostar on the north side. Do you know that that entire area was known as North Camp, which was the former barracks of the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did know about the existence of that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, please place the other map on the ELMO, the second map, the one in colour. From the south side of Mostar, and you passed by that way very often, very frequently, you had South Camp, what was known as South Camp. Once again, a former barracks of the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA. And I have marked that with JL. And the airport I have placed "Airport" there where the airport is. Do you know of the existence of that other camp, South Camp, with all the infrastructure that was constructed by the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall, though I'm a bit lost. I'm a bit lost. I don't remember that one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: From the Buna, when you entered Mostar from the south, the camp was on the left-hand side of the road facing the river Neretva.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I know the area, but I do not recall a camp there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: It was a barracks, the former JNA barracks, a large compound with residential buildings, a training centre, and so on. Do you remember it? Never mind. My last question for today: You as a professional soldier, how do you explain the fact or understand the fact that all the commands of the BH army were located among the civilian population and not housed in the barracks whether in South Camp or North Camp, although all the facilities existed. A good infrastructure existed with complete protection. So how do you as a professional army officer explain this move on the part of the BH army commanders? Did you ever wonder when you were down there why that was the case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's easy to answer. They were trying to mingle with the civilian population so as to prevent injuries and casualties among them unless the civilian population were also attack. And Your Lordship, I would like to ask a question given that I have the floor now. When I was in Mostar, when the Muslims complained of being attacked and bombarded, there was a time when they were firing from behind the hospital with howitzers. So they had behind the Muslim hospital mortars, and obviously the Croats shot back, and in thus shooting back the hospital was hit. I had to say this because I believe it is important information.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: We'll come back to that fact through two of your documents whereby you insist that mortars of the BH army move away from the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll go into that tomorrow. Mr. Registrar, can we have the blinds lowered, please. We have to do it quickly, because there's a trial in this courtroom immediately after us. Very well. Madam Usher, would you escort the gentleman out of the courtroom. Sir, you'll be back here at 9.00 for the hearing tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you asked for three minutes of our time. Go ahead quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you Your Honour, Mr. President and Your Honours. In keeping with your -- with where we left off last week in respect to cross-examination I would like to bring something to the Court and you could get back to us because there is a rule in this Tribunal under the Rules of putting your case to the witness. It's an Anglo-Saxon rule not in the United States but in other places, and it's part of the rules here. And by way of example, I wanted to share with you yesterday the gentleman was asked a question with respect to the motives of the Muslims for keeping the convoy from -- from leaving Mostar, and this is in August. And the exchange took place, just for the record, on page 32, and then it got -- he picked up again and gave us his answer on 45 and 46, and specifically on lines 18 to 22 he says the reasons why. Now, I don't want to take up too much time so I won't go into the reasons that are clearly stated on, as he put it, in the record, but then in the Prosecution document 0P 1717, which the Prosecution was reading from and taking excerpts from, on page 158, dated 31 August, 1993, there is another reason being given, and it says right here and I'm just read it very quickly: "It seems that the objective of the BH in detaining the SpaBat convoy in Mostar was to gain time to reorganise their units in the area. What they achieved was that the Croats were not putting the pressure on them during that time." Now, by way of -- I mention this for two reasons. One, I chose not to cross-examine on this particular point under the belief that since this gentleman did not write the report and the report would come in I would actually be able to make reference without there being a complaint that I was not acting due diligently by not putting the question to the witness and having him give us an explanation as to why this is in, in the particular report since he did not generate it. So I -- we need some clearance on that. When -- to what extent can we rely on not having to put questions to the witness if the document is coming in, because normally I would put the question to the witness and ask him to reconcile his explanation on the record which he says that actually they were being kept there so that the Muslims wanted to given the interns a taste of what it was like to live under those conditions versus what is in the document itself. So this is -- and I mention this because this is a time-consuming process, number one. Number two, I also use this opportunity to show how the Prosecution is cherry picking from their own documents. This is their very same document that they were making reference to. Here is a clear answer that obviously they know. They heard the gentleman give his explanation, and this is something that the Prosecution should have, in my opinion, in good faith, if we are to accept the method bona fide, put the question to the witness and say, well, here in your own document it says this. How do you reconcile it, your answer with this document? And this is my second point. And the point is on this side of the aisle because we're in an adversarial setting we simply cannot take the Prosecution at their bona fides. This is an adversarial process, this is the way it's done, and we need some guidance from the Trial Chamber. I accept the comments we made last week I'm trying to rethink my entire approach on how to cross-examine within the time constraints but this is something that I would like the Trial Chamber to at least consider and think about and give us some guidance. Not today, of course, but to just think about it. And I believe Mr. Murphy wanted to say one or two words with respect to it Eric who is leaving us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President and colleagues of the Defence -- my colleagues of the Defence have given me a very agreeable task, and that is to say a few words to Eric who has always helped us out in the best possible way, and we'd like to wish him every success in his future undertakings. And I'd also like to express the hope that his departure will not leave the Defence counsel without the facilities they need in e-court. We hope we'll not be found wanting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Well, we'll be meeting in a while, and we can go ahead. Unless Mr. Scott would like to reply to Mr. Karnavas, but quickly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Not to reply to Mr. Karnavas, Your Honour, but in line of Mr. Murphy's comments. The Prosecution would be remiss if it did not express its best wishes and thanks to Mr. Frejabue. Thank you very much and best wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I invite you back tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 30th day of August, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.51 p.m.,
